The flesh-footed shearwater Ardenna carneipes is a pelagic procellariiform seabird that breeds on islands across the Indian and Pacific Oceans. During the incubation period, eggs must be maintained at a stable thermal environment, and field measurements indicate that the average temperature of an actively incubated egg in this species is 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. At this temperature, the time from oviposition to hatching was recorded to be 54 days [ab = 54 days], a duration that aligns well with the incubation periods reported for other medium-sized shearwaters at a temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. Newly hatched chicks initially weigh approximately 99 grams [Wwb = approximately 99 grams], a figure that represents the wet weight at birth and reflects the substantial energy reserves invested by the parents into the large, yolk-rich egg. This initial mass provides a physiological foundation for the rapid somatic growth that characterizes the early nestling phase in this species.

During brooding and rearing, the chick undergoes a phase of rapid mass gain, sustained by regular provisioning of lipid-rich stomach oil and prey by both parents. Under the elevated body temperature regime typical of an active, homeothermic seabird, which is close to 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C], the nestling reaches the point of fledging after 101 days [tx = 101 days]. This interval from hatching to the achievement of first flight marks a critical developmental milestone, after which the young bird begins its transition to independence. The growth trajectory accelerates greatly during the first several weeks, and the nestling attains a peak body mass that considerably exceeds the adult mean. This maximum weight, often observed just prior to fledging, has been estimated at approximately 900 grams [Wwi = approximately 900 grams] in well-fed individuals, representing the ultimate wet weight before the bird begins to slim down for flight. The subsequent fledging interval, recorded at 101 days after hatching [tx = 101 days after hatching], provides the extended period necessary for the chick to reach full wing feather development and forage independently under the attentive guidance of its parents at a temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C].

The long developmental period for fledging at an active metabolic body temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C] of 101 days after hatching [tx = 101 days after hatching] is associated with a relatively extended phase of parental investment. With such high provisioning demands, the rate of reproductive output is necessarily constrained. Consequently, breeding pairs typically produce a single egg per nesting attempt each year [N_R_i = a single egg per nesting attempt each year], a strategy common among Procellariiformes. This annual output equates to a maximum reproductive rate of 1 egg per year [Ri = 1 egg per year], reflecting the energetic bottleneck imposed by the need to fuel chick growth to a fledging mass exceeding 900 grams [Wwi = 900 grams]. The single-egg clutch is a direct consequence of the nutritional demands required to raise a chick successfully to independence.

Following fledging, juvenile birds require a considerable period to reach physiological and anatomical maturity. Compared to other members of the Procellariidae, the flesh-footed shearwater exhibits a delayed onset of breeding readiness. Data indicate that the time since birth at the first brood for the flesh-footed shearwater is approximately 1,825 days [tR = approximately 1,825 days], a value of 5 years after hatching [tR = 5 years after hatching] being generally accepted for this species under an active metabolic temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C]. This deferred reproduction is typical of long-lived seabirds that prioritize survival and body condition in the face of unpredictable marine food resources. The onset of puberty, defined by the maturation of the gonads, occurs considerably earlier than the first successful breeding attempt.

Indeed, sexual maturation itself is achieved at a younger age than the initiation of breeding, a phenomenon common in species where social or behavioral factors delay nesting. The time since birth at puberty in Ardenna carneipes has been recorded at 303 days [tp = 303 days] when the individual is at an active body temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C]. This early gonadal development means that sub-adult birds are physiologically capable of breeding much sooner than they actually recruit into a colony, likely due to intraspecific competition for nest sites and the need to acquire foraging experience. Consistent with this life-history strategy of slow maturation and deferred reproduction, the species is also characterized by a remarkable longevity. The maximum lifespan recorded for flesh-footed shearwaters, observed in banding studies, is just over 30 years, specifically 11,023 days [am = just over 30 years, specifically 11,023 days] when the active metabolic temperature is maintained at 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C].
